idiom_name: object literal (or ES module) of factory closures
implementation_notes: A JavaScript family is a plain object whose properties are creation functions; passing that object is the entire pattern, because closures capture the family's configuration and the products only need to be duck-typed. Classes add nothing structurally: an object literal, a module namespace or a factory function returning the object all work, and the family switch is one reference swap at the composition point (or a React context/DI token holding the factory). Write down the implied product contract (JSDoc typedef or a TypeScript declaration) because nothing at runtime enforces it. For isomorphic apps (SSR + client), create the factory per request on the server and pass it as a context value; a module-level literal shared across requests leaks per-request state.
pitfalls: No type or interface enforcement: a wrong-shaped factory fails at call time, so the contract must be documented or checked at the module boundary.
Module-level object literals that close over request state leak that state between users; build the factory per request or pass the state in.
Extracting methods out of the literal breaks `this`-based implementations - prefer arrow-function fields or free functions so destructured factories keep working.

Mixing families across modules (e.g., importing DarkButton and LightSlider) cannot be caught by a linter; use an integration test that calls every factory method and asserts the product's family marker matches.
